Annual events
The <color=#3366CC>Academy Awards</color>, which honor the preceding year in film, have been held every year in late February/early March
since 2004; prior to 2004, they were held in late March/early April. Since 2002, the Oscars have been held at the Dolby
Theatre (formerly Kodak Theatre) at Hollywood Boulevard and Highland Avenue, with the exception of 2020, when due
to the <color=#3366CC>COVID-19 pandemic</color> they were held in Los Angeles Union Station.
The annual Hollywood Christmas Parade goes down Hollywood Boulevard and is broadcast in the Los Angeles area on
KTLA and around the United States on Tribune-owned stations and the WGN superstation. The 75th edition of the
parade was held in 2006.
The Hollywood Half Marathon began in 2012 and takes place every April. The event includes a Half Marathon, 10K, 5K,
and Kids Fun Run along Hollywood Blvd., and is used to raise funds and awareness for local youth homeless shelters.
Gallery
Right-wing politics
Right-wing politics, or rightism, is the range of <color=#3366CC>political ideologies</color> that view certain <color=#3366CC>social stratifications</color> and <color=#3366CC>orders</color> as
inevitable, natural, normal, or desirable, typically supporting this position in favour of <color=#3366CC>conservatism</color>, <color=#3366CC>natural law</color>,

<color=#3366CC>economics</color>, authority, <color=#3366CC>property</color>, <color=#3366CC>religion</color>, or <color=#3366CC>tradition</color>. Hierarchy and <color=#3366CC>inequality</color> may be seen as natural results of
traditional social differences or competition in <color=#3366CC>market economies</color>.
Right-wing politics are considered the counterpart to <color=#3366CC>left-wing politics</color>, and the left–right political spectrum is the most
common <color=#3366CC>political spectrum</color>. The right includes <color=#3366CC>social conservatives</color>, as well as <color=#3366CC>laissez-faire</color> economic policies. "Right"
and "right-wing" have been variously used as compliments and <color=#3366CC>pejoratives</color> describing <color=#3366CC>neoliberal</color> and conservative
economic and social ideas.
Historical overview
The political terms Left and Right were first used in the 18th century, during the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, referencing the
seating arrangement of the new National Assembly. Those who sat to the right of the chair of the presiding officer (le
président) were generally supportive of the institutions of the <color=#3366CC>monarchist</color> <color=#3366CC>Old Regime</color>. The original "Right" in France
was formed in reaction to the "Left" and comprised those supporting hierarchy, tradition, and clericalism. The
expression la droite ('the right') increased in use after the restoration of the monarchy in 1815, when it was applied to
the ultra-royalists.
<color=#3366CC>Edmund Burke</color> is regarded as one of the most influential conservative thinkers and political writers of the 18th century,
and his writings played a significant role in influencing opinions regarding conservatism following the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>
in 1789, and he remains a major figure in modern conservative and right-wing circles. Burke postulated the importance
of religious institutions for the moral stability and good of the state. He expressed his views in a satirical book, A
Vindication of Natural Society (1756). He also criticized the actions of the British government towards the <color=#3366CC>American</color>
<color=#3366CC>colonies</color>, including its taxation policies. Burke supported the American colonists' right to resist metropolitan authority.
He also supported Catholic emancipation.
While in the 19th century, Burke was praised by both conservatives and <color=#3366CC>liberals</color>, in the 20th century, Burke became
widely regarded in the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> and the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color> as the philosophical founder of conservatism. along with
his ultra-royalist and ultramontane counterpart <color=#3366CC>Joseph de Maistre</color>. His publications influenced British conservative
thought and helped establish the earliest foundations for modern conservatism.
The chief ideologue of French ultra-royalists, <color=#3366CC>Joseph de Maistre</color>, who was lawyer, diplomat, and <color=#3366CC>political philosopher</color>, is
regarded as one of intellectual forefathers of modern <color=#3366CC>conservatism</color>. Maistre was noted for his advocacy of <color=#3366CC>monarchism</color>
and <color=#3366CC>social stratification</color> in the period immediately following the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>. Maistre is also regarded as one of
the intellectual founders of the right-wing thought.
William F. Buckley Jr. was an American conservative writer and intellectual, who in 1955, founded <color=#3366CC>National Review</color>, a
magazine for the development of the conservative movement in the United States. Buckley is widely considered to
have been one of the most influential figures in the conservative movement and right-wing politics in the United States.
Positions
Anti-communism
Early <color=#3366CC>communists</color> used the term "right-wing" in reference to <color=#3366CC>conservatives</color>, placing the conservatives on the right, the
<color=#3366CC>liberals</color> in the <color=#3366CC>centre</color> and the communists on the <color=#3366CC>left</color>. Both the conservatives and the liberals were strongly
<color=#3366CC>anti-communist</color>, but the conservatives' anti-communism was much stronger than the liberals'. The history of the use of
the term right-wing in reference to anti-communism is complicated.
By <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, in most European monarchies, the divine right of kings had become discredited and was replaced by
<color=#3366CC>liberal</color> and <color=#3366CC>nationalist</color> movements. Most European monarchs became figureheads, or they yielded some of their power
to elected governments. The most conservative European monarchy, the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color>, was replaced by the
communist <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Russian Revolution</color> inspired a series of other <color=#3366CC>communist revolutions across Europe from</color>
<color=#3366CC>1917–1923</color>. Many of these revolutions, such as the <color=#3366CC>German Revolution</color>, were crushed by nationalist and monarchist
military units. During this period, nationalism was first considered right-wing, especially when it opposed the
<color=#3366CC>internationalism</color> of the communists.
After <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, communism became a global phenomenon and anti-communism became an integral part of the
domestic and foreign policies of the <color=#3366CC>United States</color> and its <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> allies. Conservatism in the post-war era abandoned
most of its monarchist and aristocratic roots, shifting its focus to patriotism, religious values, and nationalism.

Throughout the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, postcolonial governments in <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color> turned to the United States for
political and economic support. Communists were also enemies of capitalism, portraying <color=#3366CC>Wall Street</color> as the oppressor
of the masses. The United States made anti-communism the top priority of its foreign policy, and many American
conservatives sought to combat what they saw as communist influence at home. This situation led to the adoption of
several domestic policies that are collectively referred to as <color=#3366CC>McCarthyism</color>. While both liberals and conservatives were
anti-communist, the followers of <color=#3366CC>Senator McCarthy</color> were called right-wing and those on the right called liberals who
favoured free speech, even free speech for communists, leftist.

Economics
In post-revolutionary France, the Right fought against the rising power of those who had grown rich through commerce,
and sought to preserve the rights of the hereditary nobility. They were uncomfortable with capitalism, the
Enlightenment, individualism, and industrialism, and fought to retain traditional social hierarchies and institutions. In
Europe's history, there have been strong <color=#3366CC>collectivist</color> right-wing movements, such as in the social Catholic right, that
have exhibited hostility to all forms of <color=#3366CC>liberalism</color> (including <color=#3366CC>economic liberalism</color>) and have historically advocated for
paternalist class harmony involving an organic-hierarchical society where workers are protected while class hierarchy
remains.
In the 19th century, the Right had shifted to support the newly rich in some European countries (particularly Britain) and
instead of favouring the nobility over industrialists, favoured capitalists over the working class. Other right-wing
movements—such as Carlism in Spain and nationalist movements in France, Germany, and Russia—remained hostile
to capitalism and industrialism. Nevertheless, a few right-wing movements—notably the French Nouvelle Droite,
CasaPound, and American paleoconservatism—are often in opposition to capitalist ethics and the effects they have on
society. These forces see capitalism and industrialism as infringing upon or causing the decay of social traditions or
hierarchies that are essential for social order.
Laissez-faire schools
In modern times, "right-wing" is sometimes used to describe <color=#3366CC>laissez-faire capitalism</color>. In Europe, capitalists formed
alliances with the Right during their conflicts with workers after 1848. In 1871, the Austrian school came to be with the
work of <color=#3366CC>Carl Menger</color>, Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk, Friedrich von Wieser, and others, originating from methodologically
opposition to the Historical school, in a dispute known as Methodenstreit. The Austrian school opposition to be
heterodox, advocating strict adherence to methodological individualism, the concept that social phenomena result
primarily from the motivations and actions of individuals along with their self interest. Austrian-school theorists hold that
economic theory should be exclusively derived from basic principles of human action.
In France, the Right's support of capitalism can be traced to the late 19th century. The so-called <color=#3366CC>neoliberal</color> Right,

popularised by <color=#3366CC>US President</color> <color=#3366CC>Ronald Reagan</color> and UK Prime Minister <color=#3366CC>Margaret Thatcher</color>, combines support for <color=#3366CC>free</color>
<color=#3366CC>markets</color>, <color=#3366CC>privatisation</color>, and deregulation with traditional right-wing support for social conformity.
Nationalism
In France, <color=#3366CC>nationalism</color> was originally a left-wing and republican ideology. After the period of boulangisme and the
<color=#3366CC>Dreyfus affair</color>, nationalism became a trait of the right wing. Right-wing nationalists sought to define and defend a "true"
national identity from elements which they believed were corrupting that identity. Some were <color=#3366CC>supremacists</color>, who in
accordance with <color=#3366CC>scientific racism</color> and <color=#3366CC>social Darwinism</color> applied the concept of "survival of the fittest" to <color=#3366CC>nations</color> and
<color=#3366CC>races</color>.
Right-wing nationalism was influenced by Romantic nationalism in which the state derives its political legitimacy from
the organic unity of those who it governs. This generally includes the language, race, culture, religion, and customs of
the nation, all of which were "born" within its culture. Linked with right-wing nationalism is cultural conservatism, which
supports the preservation of the heritage of a nation or culture and often sees deviations from cultural norms as an
existential threat.
In the 21st century, neo-nationalism came to prominence after the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Western world</color>. It is typically
associated with cultural conservatism, <color=#3366CC>populism</color>, anti-globalisation, and nativism and is opposed to immigration. The
<color=#3366CC>ideology</color> takes historical association in determining membership in a nation, rather than <color=#3366CC>racial concepts</color>.
Natural law and traditionalism
Right-wing politics typically justifies a hierarchical society based on <color=#3366CC>natural law</color> or <color=#3366CC>tradition</color>.
Traditionalism was advocated by a group of United States university professors (labelled the "New Conservatives" by

the popular press) who rejected the concepts of <color=#3366CC>individualism</color>, <color=#3366CC>liberalism</color>, <color=#3366CC>modernity</color>, and <color=#3366CC>social progress</color>, seeking
instead to promote what they identified as cultural and educational renewal.
Populism
<color=#3366CC>Right-wing populism</color> is a combination of civic-nationalism, cultural-nationalism and sometimes ethno-nationalism,
localism, along with anti-elitism, using populist rhetoric to provide a critique of existing political institutions. According to
Margaret Canovan, a right-wing populist is "a charismatic leader, using the tactics of politicians' populism to go past the
politicians and intellectual elite and appeal to the reactionary sentiments of the populace, often buttressing his claim to
speak for the people by the use of referendums".
In Europe, right-wing populism often takes the form of distrust of the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> (commonly known as
Euroscepticism), and of politicians in general, combined with anti-immigrant rhetoric and a call for a return to traditional,
national values. Daniel Stockemer states, the radical right is, "Targeting immigrants as a threat to employment, security
and cultural cohesion".
In the United States, the <color=#3366CC>Tea Party movement</color> stated that the core beliefs for membership were the primacy of
individual liberties as defined by the Constitution of the United States, preference for a small federal government, and
respect for the rule of law. Some policy positions included opposition to illegal immigration and support for a strong
national military force, the right to individual gun ownership, cutting taxes, reducing government spending, and
balancing the budget.
In Indonesia, Islamic populism has a significant impact on right-wing politics. This is largely due to the historical context
which Islamic organisations had during the 1960s in destroying the Indonesian Communist Party. Whilst the party is
adopting democratic processes with neo-liberal market economies, socially pluralist positions are not necessarily
adopted. The Islamic populism in Indonesia has boosted its influence in 1998 after the demise of the Suharto
authoritarian regime. Islamic populism in Indonesia has similar properties with Islamic populist regimes like in the
Middle East, Turkey and North Africa (MENA). The emphasis on social justice, pluralism, equality and progressive
agendas could be potentially mobilised by Islamic cultural resources.
In India, supporters of the <color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata Party</color> (BJP) have more authoritarian, nativist, and populist ideas than other
Indian citizens. Under Narendra Modi, populism is a core part of the party's ideology. The party's rhetoric reflects the
idea is that the ordinary, "good" individuals are continuously under attack from "bad" political forces, the media, etc.
Since Narendra Modi became the leader of the BJP, it has increasingly been considered a populist radical right party
(PRR) and has also been considered a Hindu nationalist party.
Religion

In <color=#3366CC>The Possessed</color> (1872) and <color=#3366CC>The Brothers Karamazov</color> (1880), <color=#3366CC>Fyodor Dostoevsky</color> portrayed <color=#3366CC>socialism</color> as an attempt
to build a kingdom of Man as opposed to the <color=#3366CC>kingdom of God</color>. According to Dostoevsky, the intention of the latter book
was to portray "the seed of the idea of destruction in our time in Russia among the young people uprooted from reality".
This seed is depicted as: "the rejection not of God but of the meaning of His creation. Socialism has sprung from the
denial of the meaning of historical reality and ended in a programme of destruction and anarchism". In his 1931
encyclical Quadragesimo Anno, Pope Pius XI wrote that "true socialism" was irreconcilable with the teachings of the
<color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> "because its concept of society itself is utterly foreign to Christian truth", stating:
"For, according to Christian teaching, man, endowed with a social nature, is placed on this earth so that by leading a
life in society and under an authority ordained of God he may fully cultivate and develop all his faculties unto the praise
and glory of his Creator; and that by faithfully fulfilling the duties of his craft or other calling he may obtain for himself
temporal and at the same time eternal happiness. Socialism, on the other hand, wholly ignoring and indifferent to this
sublime end of both man and society, affirms that human association has been instituted for the sake of material
advantage alone"
American right-wing media outlets oppose sex outside marriage and <color=#3366CC>same-sex marriage</color>, and they sometimes reject
scientific positions on <color=#3366CC>evolution</color> and other matters where science is perceived to disagree with the <color=#3366CC>Bible</color>.
The term family values has been used by right-wing parties—such as the <color=#3366CC>Republican Party</color> in the United States, the
Family First Party in Australia, the <color=#3366CC>Conservative Party</color> in the United Kingdom, and the <color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata Party</color> in
India—to signify support for traditional families and opposition to the changes which the modern world has made in

relation to how families live. Supporters of "family values" may oppose <color=#3366CC>abortion</color>, <color=#3366CC>euthanasia</color>, <color=#3366CC>birth control</color> and <color=#3366CC>same-sex</color>
<color=#3366CC>marriage</color>.
Outside the <color=#3366CC>West</color>, the Hindu nationalist movement has attracted privileged groups which fear encroachment on their
dominant positions, as well as "plebeian" and impoverished groups which seek recognition around a majoritarian
rhetoric of cultural pride, order, and national strength.
In <color=#3366CC>Israel</color>, <color=#3366CC>Meir Kahane</color> advocated the belief that Israel should be a <color=#3366CC>theocratic state</color>, preferably, a Halachic state where
non-<color=#3366CC>Jews</color> should have no voting rights, and the far-right organization Lehava strictly opposes Jewish assimilation and
the Christian presence in Israel. In the United States, the <color=#3366CC>FBI</color> classified the Jewish Defence League (JDL) as "a right
wing terrorist group" in 2001. Many <color=#3366CC>Islamist</color> groups have been called right-wing, including the Great Union Party, the
Combatant Clergy Association/Association of Militant Clergy, and the Islamic Society of Engineers of Iran.
Social stratification
Right-wing politics involves, to varying degrees, the rejection of some <color=#3366CC>egalitarian</color> objectives of <color=#3366CC>left-wing politics</color>, based
on the belief that <color=#3366CC>social</color> or <color=#3366CC>economic inequality</color> is natural and inevitable or the belief that it is beneficial to society.
Right-wing ideologies and movements support <color=#3366CC>social order</color>. The original French right-wing was called "the party of
order" because it believed that France needed to be ruled by a strong political leader who would keep order.
The conservative British scholar R. J. White, who rejects egalitarianism, wrote: "Men are equal before God and the
laws, but they are unequal in all else; hierarchy is the order of nature, and privilege is the reward of honourable
service". American conservative Russell Kirk also rejected egalitarianism as imposing sameness, stating: "Men are
created different; and a government that ignores this law becomes an unjust government for it sacrifices nobility to
mediocrity". Italian scholar Norberto Bobbio argued that the right-wing is inegalitarian compared to the left-wing,
because he argued that equality is a relative, not an absolute, concept.
Right-libertarians reject <color=#3366CC>collective</color> or <color=#3366CC>state-imposed equality</color> as undermining rewards for <color=#3366CC>personal merits</color>, initiatives, and
enterprise. In their view, such imposed equality is unjust, limits personal freedom, and leads to social uniformity and
mediocrity.
In the view of philosopher Jason Stanley in How Fascism Works, the "politics of hierarchy" is one of the hallmarks of
<color=#3366CC>fascism</color>, which refers to a "glorious past" in which members of the rightfully dominant group sat atop the hierarchy, and
attempt to recreate this state of being.
History
According to The Cambridge History of Twentieth-Century Political Thought (2003), the Right has gone through five
distinct historical stages:
• The reactionary right sought a return to <color=#3366CC>aristocracy</color> and <color=#3366CC>established religion</color>.
• The moderate right distrusted intellectuals and advocated the establishment of limited governments.
• The <color=#3366CC>radical right</color> espoused a romantic and an aggressive form of nationalism.
• The extreme right explicitly advocated the implementation of anti-immigration policies and it implicitly espoused
<color=#3366CC>racism</color>.
• The <color=#3366CC>neo-liberal</color> right sought to combine a market economy and economic deregulation with the traditional
right-wing beliefs in <color=#3366CC>patriotism</color>, elitism and law and order.
From the 1830s to the 1880s, the <color=#3366CC>Western world</color>'s <color=#3366CC>social class</color> structure and economy shifted from <color=#3366CC>nobility</color> and

<color=#3366CC>aristocracy</color> towards <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>. This shift affected <color=#3366CC>centre-right</color> movements such as the <color=#3366CC>British Conservative Party</color>, which
responded supporting capitalism.
The populations of English-speaking countries did not apply the terms right and left to their politics until the 20th
century. The term right-wing was originally applied to traditional conservatives, <color=#3366CC>monarchists</color>, and reactionaries; a
revision of this which occurred sometime between the 1920s and 1950s considers the <color=#3366CC>far-right</color> to denote <color=#3366CC>fascism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Nazism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>racial supremacy</color>.
Rightist regimes were common in Europe during the <color=#3366CC>Interwar period</color>, 1919–1938.
China
Republic of China (1912–1949)
Among <color=#3366CC>Kuomintang</color> (KMT)'s conservatives during the <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color>, Dai Jitao and Hu Hanmin supporters formed
the right-wing Western Hills Group in the <color=#3366CC>1920s</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Chiang Kai-shek</color> initially claimed himself as a 'centrist' in the KMT left-right conflict, but became an anti-communist
right-wing after <color=#3366CC>Shanghai massacre</color>. Within the Kuomintang, both right-wing and left-wing factions existed, but the
National Revolutionary Army was Chiang's led by the right-wing Kuomintang.
People's Republic of China
Neoauthoritarianism is a current of political thought that rose in China in the late 1980s and came into ascendancy after
the death of <color=#3366CC>Deng Xiaoping</color>; it advocates a powerful state to facilitate <color=#3366CC>market reforms</color>. It has been described as
right-wing, classically conservative even though it incorporated some aspects of <color=#3366CC>Marxist–Leninist</color> and <color=#3366CC>Maoist</color> theories.
Since Xi took office as CCP general secretary and became the top leader in November 2012, <color=#3366CC>social conservatism</color> has
been strengthened, including the traditional gender role for women and accelerated crackdown on <color=#3366CC>LGBTQ+ activism</color>.
Within a western context, the <color=#3366CC>Chinese Communist Party</color> does not fit neatly into either left or right-wing traditions;
however, it has been characterized by scholars as adapting views and policies closely related to the authoritarian right,
particularly on socio-cultural issues as well as <color=#3366CC>foreign policy</color>.
France
Throughout France in the 19th century, the main line dividing the left and right was between supporters of the republic
and those of the monarchy, who were often secularist and Catholic respectively.
Hungary
The dominance of the political right of inter-war Hungary, after the collapse of a short-lived Communist regime, was
described by historian István Deák: Between 1919 and 1944 Hungary was a rightist country. Forged out of a
counter-revolutionary heritage, its governments advocated a "nationalist Christian" policy; they extolled heroism, faith,
and unity; they despised the French Revolution, and they spurned the liberal and socialist ideologies of the 19th
century. The governments saw Hungary as a bulwark against bolshevism and bolshevism's instruments: <color=#3366CC>socialism</color>,
<color=#3366CC>cosmopolitanism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Freemasonry</color>. They perpetrated the rule of a small clique of aristocrats, civil servants, and army
officers, and surrounded with adulation the head of the state, the counterrevolutionary <color=#3366CC>Admiral Horthy</color>.
India
Although freedom fighters are favoured, the right-wing tendency to elect or appoint politicians and government officials
based on aristocratic and religious ties is common to almost all the states of India. Multiple political parties, however,
identify with terms and beliefs which are, by political consensus, right- or left-wing. Certain political parties such as the
<color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata Party</color>, identify with conservative and nationalist elements. Some, such as the <color=#3366CC>Indian National</color>
<color=#3366CC>Congress</color>, take a liberal stance. The Communist Party of India, Communist Party of India (Marxist), and others, identify
with left-wing socialist and communist concepts. Other political parties take differing stands, and hence cannot be
clearly grouped as the left and the right wing.

United Kingdom
In British politics, the terms right and left came into common use for the first time in the late 1930s during debates over
the <color=#3366CC>Spanish Civil War</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Conservative Party</color>, one of the country's two main political parties, is placed on the centre-right to right-wing of the
left–right political spectrum. Reform UK is situated on the right wing of the political spectrum, generally to the
Conservative Party's right.
United States
In the United States, following the <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color>, social conservatives joined forces with right-wing elements of the
<color=#3366CC>Republican Party</color> to gain support among traditionally <color=#3366CC>Democratic</color> voting populations like white southerners and
Catholics. <color=#3366CC>Ronald Reagan</color>'s election to the presidency in 1980 cemented the alliance between the religious right in the
United States and social conservatives.
In 2019, the United States populace leaned <color=#3366CC>centre-right</color>, with 37% of Americans self-identifying as conservative,
compared to 35% moderate and 24% liberal. This was continuing a decades-long trend of the country leaning
centre-right.
The United States Department of Homeland Security defines right-wing extremism in the United States as "broadly
divided into those groups, movements, and adherents that are primarily hate-oriented (based on hatred of particular
religious, racial or ethnic groups), and those that are mainly anti-government, rejecting federal authority in favour of
state or local authority, or rejecting government authority entirely. It may include groups and individuals that are
dedicated to a single issue, such as opposition to abortion or immigration".
Types
The meaning of right-wing "varies across societies, historical epochs, and political systems and ideologies". According
to The Concise Oxford Dictionary of Politics, in liberal democracies, the political right opposes <color=#3366CC>socialism</color> and <color=#3366CC>social</color>

<color=#3366CC>democracy</color>. Right-wing parties include <color=#3366CC>conservatives</color>, <color=#3366CC>Christian democrats</color>, <color=#3366CC>classical liberals</color>, and <color=#3366CC>nationalists</color>, as well
as <color=#3366CC>fascists</color> on the <color=#3366CC>far-right</color>.
British academics Noël O'Sullivan and Roger Eatwell divide the right into five types: reactionary, moderate, radical,
extreme, and new. Chip Berlet wrote that each of these "styles of thought" are "responses to the left", including
liberalism and socialism, which have arisen since the 1789 French Revolution.
• The reactionary right looks toward the past and is "aristocratic, religious and authoritarian".
• The <color=#3366CC>moderate right</color>, typified by the writings of <color=#3366CC>Edmund Burke</color>, is tolerant of change, provided it is gradual and
accepts some aspects of liberalism, including the rule of law and capitalism, although it sees radical <color=#3366CC>laissez-faire</color>
and individualism as harmful to society. The moderate right often promotes nationalism and social welfare policies.
• Radical right is a descriptive term that was developed after World War II and it was applied to groups and
ideologies such as <color=#3366CC>McCarthyism</color>, the John Birch Society, Thatcherism, and the Republikaner Party. Eatwell
stresses that this usage of the term has "major typological problems" because it "has also been applied to clearly
democratic developments". The radical right includes <color=#3366CC>right-wing populism</color> and various other subtypes.
• The <color=#3366CC>extreme right</color> has four traits: "1) anti-democracy, 2) ultranationalism, 3) <color=#3366CC>racism</color>, and 4) the strong state".
• The New Right consists of the <color=#3366CC>liberal conservatives</color>, who stress small government, <color=#3366CC>free markets</color>, and individual
initiative.
Other authors make a distinction between the centre-right and the far-right.
• Parties of the centre-right generally support <color=#3366CC>liberal democracy</color>, <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>, the <color=#3366CC>market economy</color> (though they may
accept government regulation to control monopolies), <color=#3366CC>private property</color> rights, and a limited welfare state (for
example, government provision of education and medical care). They support conservatism and economic
liberalism and oppose socialism and communism.
• By contrast, the phrase "far-right" is used to describe those who favour an absolutist government, which uses the
power of the state to support the dominant ethnic group or religion and criminalise other ethnic groups or religions.
Typical examples of leaders to whom the far-right label is often applied are: <color=#3366CC>Francisco Franco</color> in <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Benito</color>

<color=#3366CC>Mussolini</color> in <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Adolf Hitler</color> in <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Augusto Pinochet</color> in <color=#3366CC>Chile</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Jorge Rafael Videla</color> in <color=#3366CC>Argentina</color>.
